extended_nodes_v2.label: Initial Product Requirements Meeting
extended_nodes_v2.description: Conversation between ML engineer (candidate) and Product Manager establishing requirements

dialogue.speaker: Product Manager
dialogue.text: We're seeing 45% of phishing attacks get through to users. That's causing about $20M in fraud losses annually. We need an ML model to catch at least 70% of these attacks.

dialogue.speaker: ML Engineer (Candidate)
dialogue.text: Got it. What's the user experience? Are we blocking sites outright or showing warnings?

dialogue.speaker: Product Manager
dialogue.text: Browser extension warning. Users can still proceed, but we want to catch their attention. Critical constraint: false positives must stay under 5%. Above that, we'll drown in support tickets.

dialogue.speaker: ML Engineer
dialogue.text: Understood. So 70% recall minimum, 5% FPR maximum. What about latency? This is real-time classification?

dialogue.speaker: Product Manager
dialogue.text: Yes, real-time. User visits a site, we classify within 100ms or they'll notice lag. Also, Legal wants explainability—users need to understand why a site was flagged if they appeal.

dialogue.speaker: ML Engineer
dialogue.text: Perfect. Let me confirm the constraints: (1) Recall ≥ 70%, (2) FPR ≤ 5%, (3) Latency < 100ms, (4) Explainable decisions. ROC AUC ≥ 0.80 as overall performance metric. Does that capture it?

dialogue.speaker: Product Manager
dialogue.text: Exactly. When can you have a baseline?

dialogue.speaker: ML Engineer
dialogue.text: Two weeks for EDA and baseline models. I'll document findings and share preliminary results midpoint. Sound good?

extended_nodes_v2.outcome: Clear KPI agreement: Recall ≥ 70%, FPR ≤ 5%, ROC AUC ≥ 0.80. Explainability and latency constraints documented.
communication_best_practices: Propose concrete timeline (2 weeks) vs vague 'soon'

extended_nodes_v2.label: Legal Explainability Requirements Discussion
extended_nodes_v2.description: Conversation clarifying GDPR Article 22 compliance and explainability depth needed

dialogue.speaker: Legal Officer
dialogue.text: Under GDPR Article 22, users have the right to understand automated decisions. If we block a site, we need to explain why in terms users can understand.

dialogue.speaker: ML Engineer
dialogue.text: Understood. What level of detail? Do you need coefficient-based models, or can we use SHAP values for complex models like XGBoost?

dialogue.speaker: Legal Officer
dialogue.text: What's the difference for a non-technical user?

dialogue.speaker: ML Engineer
dialogue.text: Coefficient-based: 'Site flagged because domain is 2 months old (high risk) and has no external references (suspicious).' SHAP: Same explanation but generated via model-agnostic interpretation. Both human-readable, but SHAP allows more complex models.

dialogue.speaker: Legal Officer
dialogue.text: SHAP is fine if it's human-readable. I need reports that say: 'This site was flagged because: Factor 1 (domain age) contributed +30% risk, Factor 2 (no HTTPS) contributed +25% risk...' Can you do that?

dialogue.speaker: ML Engineer
dialogue.text: Yes. SHAP generates exactly that—contribution of each feature to the final decision. I'll include it in the API response and log it for audit trails.

dialogue.speaker: Legal Officer
dialogue.text: Perfect. Also, we need to test for bias. Can your model discriminate against startups with new domains?

dialogue.speaker: ML Engineer
dialogue.text: Valid concern. I'll run fairness audits: stratify false positive rates by industry and domain age. If startups have significantly higher FPR, we'll adjust thresholds or retrain.

extended_nodes_v2.outcome: SHAP explainability approved. Fairness audit required (FPR by industry/domain age). Audit trail logging mandatory.
compliance_requirements: Feature contribution report for every blocked site
Fairness metrics: FPR by protected groups (startups, industries)
Audit trail: 2-year retention of decisions + explanations

extended_nodes_v2.label: Complete Gradient Descent Derivation with L2
extended_nodes_v2.description: Full mathematical derivation from cross-entropy loss to gradient descent update rule with L2 regularization

proof.label: Loss Function Definition
proof.equation: L(θ) = -(1/m) Σ[y_i log(σ(x_i^T θ)) + (1-y_i) log(1-σ(x_i^T θ))] + (λ/2m) ||θ||²
proof.description: Cross-entropy loss (first term) + L2 regularization penalty (second term). m = number of samples, λ = regularization strength, σ = sigmoid function.

proof.label: Sigmoid Function
proof.description: Logistic function mapping real numbers to (0,1) probabilities.

proof.label: Partial Derivative of Loss w.r.t θ_j
proof.description: Apply chain rule: ∂L/∂θ_j = ∂L/∂σ × ∂σ/∂z × ∂z/∂θ_j. Note: z_i = x_i^T θ, so ∂z_i/∂θ_j = x_{ij}.

proof.label: Simplify using σ'(z) = σ(z)(1-σ(z))
proof.description: Substitute σ'(z_i) = σ(z_i)(1-σ(z_i)) and cancel terms.

proof.label: Final Gradient
proof.description: Factor out and simplify: y_i(1-σ) - (1-y_i)σ = y_i - y_i σ - σ + y_i σ = y_i - σ = -(σ - y_i).

proof.label: Vectorized Gradient
proof.description: Matrix form: X is (m × n) feature matrix, θ is (n × 1) weights, y is (m × 1) labels, σ(Xθ) is (m × 1) predictions.

proof.label: Gradient Descent Update
proof.equation: θ := θ - α ∇L(θ) = θ - α [(1/m) X^T (σ(Xθ) - y) + (λ/m) θ]
proof.description: Update rule: Move weights in direction opposite to gradient. α = learning rate (step size).

proof.label: L2 Regularization Interpretation
proof.bayesian_view: L2 penalty λ||θ||²/2 equivalent to MAP estimation with Gaussian prior p(θ) ~ N(0, 1/λ). Larger λ → stronger prior belief that weights should be small.
proof.weight_decay_view: Update can be rewritten as: θ := (1 - αλ/m)θ - α(1/m)X^T(σ(Xθ) - y). Factor (1 - αλ/m) < 1 shrinks weights toward zero each iteration (weight decay).

numerical_stability_notes: For z >> 0: σ(z) ≈ 1, log(σ(z)) ≈ 0. Use log(1 + exp(-z)) instead of log(exp(z)/(1+exp(z))) to avoid overflow.
For z << 0: σ(z) ≈ 0, log(1-σ(z)) ≈ 0. Use log(1 + exp(z)) symmetrically.
Add epsilon=1e-15 to predictions before log: log(pred + eps) to prevent log(0) = -∞.

extended_nodes_v2.label: NumPy Gradient Descent Implementation
extended_nodes_v2.description: Production-quality Python implementation with error handling, logging, early stopping
extended_nodes_v2.code:
import numpy as np
import logging
from typing import Tuple, Optional

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class LogisticRegressionGD:
    """Logistic Regression with Gradient Descent and L2 regularization.
    
    Implements full-batch gradient descent with early stopping.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    learning_rate : float, default=0.1
        Step size for gradient descent updates.
    max_epochs : int, default=120
        Maximum number of training iterations.
    l2_lambda : float, default=0.001
        L2 regularization strength. Higher values → stronger regularization.
    convergence_threshold : float, default=1e-4
        Training stops if loss change < threshold for consecutive epochs.
    patience : int, default=10
        Number of epochs to wait for improvement before early stopping.
    random_state : int, optional
        Seed for weight initialization reproducibility.
    
    Attributes
    ----------
    theta : np.ndarray, shape (n_features,)
        Learned weight vector.
    loss_history : list
        Training loss at each epoch.
    converged : bool
        True if training converged before max_epochs.
    """
    
    def __init__(
        self,
        learning_rate: float = 0.1,
        max_epochs: int = 120,
        l2_lambda: float = 0.001,
        convergence_threshold: float = 1e-4,
        patience: int = 10,
        random_state: Optional[int] = None
    ):
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate
        self.max_epochs = max_epochs
        self.l2_lambda = l2_lambda
        self.convergence_threshold = convergence_threshold
        self.patience = patience
        self.random_state = random_state
        
        self.theta = None
        self.loss_history = []
        self.converged = False
        
    def _sigmoid(self, z: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Numerically stable sigmoid function.
        
        Prevents overflow by splitting positive/negative cases.
        """
        # Clip to prevent overflow in exp
        z = np.clip(z, -500, 500)
        
        # For positive z: σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
        # For negative z: σ(z) = exp(z) / (1 + exp(z)) = 1 - σ(-z)
        pos_mask = z >= 0
        neg_mask = ~pos_mask
        
        sigmoid = np.zeros_like(z)
        sigmoid[pos_mask] = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z[pos_mask]))
        sigmoid[neg_mask] = np.exp(z[neg_mask]) / (1 + np.exp(z[neg_mask]))
        
        return sigmoid
    
    def _compute_loss(
        self,
        X: np.ndarray,
        y: np.ndarray,
        predictions: np.ndarray
    ) -> float:
        """Cross-entropy loss with L2 regularization.
        
        L(θ) = -(1/m) Σ[y log(σ) + (1-y) log(1-σ)] + (λ/2m)||θ||²
        """
        m = len(y)
        epsilon = 1e-15  # Numerical stability
        
        # Clip predictions to [epsilon, 1-epsilon]
        predictions = np.clip(predictions, epsilon, 1 - epsilon)
        
        # Cross-entropy loss
        ce_loss = -(1/m) * np.sum(
            y * np.log(predictions) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - predictions)
        )
        
        # L2 regularization (don't penalize bias term theta[0] if exists)
        l2_penalty = (self.l2_lambda / (2 * m)) * np.sum(self.theta**2)
        
        return ce_loss + l2_penalty
    
    def fit(self, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> 'LogisticRegressionGD':
        """Train logistic regression using gradient descent.
        
        Parameters
        ----------
        X : np.ndarray, shape (m, n)
            Training features. m samples, n features.
        y : np.ndarray, shape (m,)
            Binary labels (0 or 1).
            
        Returns
        -------
        self : LogisticRegressionGD
            Fitted estimator.
        """
        m, n = X.shape
        
        # Validate inputs
        assert y.shape[0] == m, f"X and y length mismatch: {m} vs {y.shape[0]}"
        assert set(y).issubset({0, 1}), "y must be binary (0 or 1)"
        
        # Initialize weights
        if self.random_state is not None:
            np.random.seed(self.random_state)
        self.theta = np.random.normal(0, 0.01, size=n)  # Small random init
        
        logger.info(f"Training started: {m} samples, {n} features")
        logger.info(f"Hyperparameters: lr={self.learning_rate}, lambda={self.l2_lambda}")
        
        # Training loop
        no_improvement_count = 0
        best_loss = float('inf')
        
        for epoch in range(self.max_epochs):
            # Forward pass
            z = X @ self.theta
            predictions = self._sigmoid(z)
            
            # Compute loss
            loss = self._compute_loss(X, y, predictions)
            self.loss_history.append(loss)
            
            # Compute gradient: ∇L = (1/m)X^T(σ(Xθ) - y) + (λ/m)θ
            error = predictions - y
            gradient = (1/m) * (X.T @ error) + (self.l2_lambda / m) * self.theta
            
            # Update weights: θ := θ - α∇L
            self.theta -= self.learning_rate * gradient
            
            # Logging
            if epoch % 20 == 0:
                grad_norm = np.linalg.norm(gradient)
                logger.info(
                    f"Epoch {epoch}/{self.max_epochs}: "
                    f"Loss={loss:.6f}, GradNorm={grad_norm:.6f}"
                )
            
            # Early stopping check
            if epoch > 0:
                loss_change = abs(self.loss_history[-2] - loss)
                
                if loss < best_loss:
                    best_loss = loss
                    no_improvement_count = 0
                else:
                    no_improvement_count += 1
                
                if loss_change < self.convergence_threshold:
                    if no_improvement_count >= self.patience:
                        self.converged = True
                        logger.info(
                            f"Converged at epoch {epoch}. "
                            f"Loss change: {loss_change:.2e} < {self.convergence_threshold:.2e}"
                        )
                        break
        
        if not self.converged:
            logger.warning(
                f"Did not converge after {self.max_epochs} epochs. "
                f"Final loss: {loss:.6f}. Consider increasing max_epochs or learning_rate."
            )
        
        return self
    
    def predict_proba(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Predict class probabilities.
        
        Parameters
        ----------
        X : np.ndarray, shape (m, n)
            Test features.
            
        Returns
        -------
        proba : np.ndarray, shape (m, 2)
            Class probabilities. [:, 0] = P(y=0), [:, 1] = P(y=1).
        """
        if self.theta is None:
            raise ValueError("Model not fitted. Call fit() first.")
        
        z = X @ self.theta
        p_positive = self._sigmoid(z)
        p_negative = 1 - p_positive
        
        return np.column_stack([p_negative, p_positive])
    
    def predict(self, X: np.ndarray, threshold: float = 0.5) -> np.ndarray:
        """Predict binary class labels.
        
        Parameters
        ----------
        X : np.ndarray, shape (m, n)
            Test features.
        threshold : float, default=0.5
            Classification threshold. P(y=1) >= threshold → predict 1.
            
        Returns
        -------
        predictions : np.ndarray, shape (m,)
            Binary predictions (0 or 1).
        """
        proba = self.predict_proba(X)
        return (proba[:, 1] >= threshold).astype(int)


# Usage example
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Configure logging
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    
    # Load data (assuming preprocessed)
    from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
    X_train, y_train = make_classification(
        n_samples=8000, n_features=20, n_informative=15,
        n_redundant=5, random_state=42
    )
    
    # Train model
    model = LogisticRegressionGD(
        learning_rate=0.1,
        max_epochs=120,
        l2_lambda=0.001,
        random_state=42
    )
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    
    # Predict
    y_pred = model.predict(X_train)
    accuracy = (y_pred == y_train).mean()
    print(f"Training accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")
    
    # Plot loss curve
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    plt.plot(model.loss_history)
    plt.xlabel('Epoch')
    plt.ylabel('Loss')
    plt.title('Training Loss Curve')
    plt.savefig('results/training_loss.png')

extended_nodes_v2.label: Edge Cases in Clipping Negative Values
extended_nodes_v2.description: Comprehensive error handling for impossible negative values in NoOfImage

edge_cases.scenario: Entire dataset has NoOfImage < 0 (extreme data corruption)
edge_cases.detection: if (df['NoOfImage'] < 0).all(): raise ValueError('All NoOfImage values negative—data corruption suspected')
edge_cases.handling: Abort pipeline, log error, alert data engineering team. Do NOT proceed with clipping—requires data investigation.
edge_cases.rationale: If all values corrupt, dataset unusable. Clipping would mask systemic issue.

edge_cases.scenario: 377 negative values all in first 1000 rows (not random)
edge_cases.detection: negative_indices = df[df['NoOfImage'] < 0].index; if len(set(negative_indices[:100])) < 10: log_warning('Negatives clustered')
edge_cases.handling: Investigate pattern: Are these all from same data source? Same date range? May indicate specific ETL bug.
edge_cases.example: Rows 1-377 all negative → Suspect data generation script bug (loop starting at -377?).

edge_cases.handling: Check if -9999 is sentinel for missing data. If yes, convert to NaN, then impute. If no, clip to 0.
edge_cases.rationale: Sentinel values (e.g., -9999, -1) sometimes used in raw data to indicate 'missing' rather than 'impossible'.

edge_cases.case: Negative values paired with NULL in other features
edge_cases.scenario: All rows with NoOfImage < 0 also have IsResponsive = NULL
edge_cases.detection: negative_mask = df['NoOfImage'] < 0; null_mask = df['IsResponsive'].isnull(); if (negative_mask == null_mask).mean() > 0.9: log_warning('Negatives correlated with NULLs')
edge_cases.handling: Likely systematic data issue (e.g., scraping failure). Consider dropping these rows entirely if data quality suspect.
edge_cases.example: Scraper failed → returned NoOfImage=-1, IsResponsive=NULL. Better to drop than impute low-quality samples.

validation_checks: assert df.shape[0] == pre_clip_row_count, 'Clipping dropped rows (should not happen)'
extended_nodes_v2.logging_example: logger.info(f'Clipped {negative_count} negative NoOfImage values to 0. Range before: [{df['NoOfImage'].min()}, {df['NoOfImage'].max()}], after: [{df_clipped['NoOfImage'].min()}, {df_clipped['NoOfImage'].max()}]')
extended_nodes_v2.rollback_plan: If clipping causes downstream issues (e.g., model performance drops), revert to pre-clip state: df['NoOfImage'] = df['NoOfImage_backup']. Re-evaluate imputation strategy.

extended_nodes_v2.label: Unit Tests for Gradient Descent
extended_nodes_v2.description: Comprehensive test suite validating gradient computation correctness

test_suite.description: Validate gradient via finite differences: ∇L ≈ [L(θ+ε) - L(θ-ε)] / 2ε
test_suite.method: For each weight θ_j, perturb by ε=1e-5, compute loss, estimate gradient. Compare to analytical gradient.
test_suite.code:
def test_gradient_numerical_approximation():
    X = np.random.randn(100, 5)
    y = np.random.randint(0, 2, 100)
    model = LogisticRegressionGD()
    model.theta = np.random.randn(5)
    
    # Analytical gradient
    z = X @ model.theta
    pred = model._sigmoid(z)
    analytical_grad = (1/100) * X.T @ (pred - y)
    
    # Numerical gradient
    epsilon = 1e-5
    numerical_grad = np.zeros(5)
    for j in range(5):
        theta_plus = model.theta.copy()
        theta_plus[j] += epsilon
        loss_plus = model._compute_loss(X, y, model._sigmoid(X @ theta_plus))
        
        theta_minus = model.theta.copy()
        theta_minus[j] -= epsilon
        loss_minus = model._compute_loss(X, y, model._sigmoid(X @ theta_minus))
        
        numerical_grad[j] = (loss_plus - loss_minus) / (2 * epsilon)
    
    # Assert close (within 1e-4 relative error)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(analytical_grad, numerical_grad, rtol=1e-4)
test_suite.rationale: If analytical gradient implementation wrong, finite differences will differ. This catches mathematical errors.

test_suite.description: Compare custom implementation to sklearn LogisticRegression on same data
test_suite.code:
def test_sklearn_parity():
    from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression as SklearnLR
    
    X_train, y_train = make_classification(n_samples=500, n_features=10, random_state=42)
    
    # Custom model
    custom = LogisticRegressionGD(learning_rate=0.1, l2_lambda=0.001, random_state=42)
    custom.fit(X_train, y_train)
    custom_pred = custom.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]
    
    # Sklearn model (C = 1/lambda for L2)
    sklearn = SklearnLR(penalty='l2', C=1/0.001, solver='lbfgs', random_state=42)
    sklearn.fit(X_train, y_train)
    sklearn_pred = sklearn.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]
    
    # Predictions should correlate highly (r > 0.99)
    from scipy.stats import pearsonr
    corr, _ = pearsonr(custom_pred, sklearn_pred)
    assert corr > 0.99, f'Low correlation: {corr:.4f}'
    
    # AUC should be within 0.01
    from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
    auc_custom = roc_auc_score(y_train, custom_pred)
    auc_sklearn = roc_auc_score(y_train, sklearn_pred)
    assert abs(auc_custom - auc_sklearn) < 0.01, f'AUC diff: {abs(auc_custom - auc_sklearn):.4f}'
test_suite.rationale: sklearn battle-tested. If custom implementation differs significantly, likely has bugs.

test_suite.description: Linearly separable toy data should converge to near-zero loss
test_suite.code:
def test_convergence_on_toy_data():
    # Linearly separable data
    X = np.array([[1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3], [1, 2], [2, 3]])
    y = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1])
    
    model = LogisticRegressionGD(learning_rate=0.5, max_epochs=500, l2_lambda=0)
    model.fit(X, y)
    
    # Should achieve near-perfect classification
    pred = model.predict(X)
    accuracy = (pred == y).mean()
    assert accuracy >= 0.95, f'Low accuracy on toy data: {accuracy:.2f}'
    
    # Final loss should be small
    assert model.loss_history[-1] < 0.1, f'Loss did not converge: {model.loss_history[-1]:.4f}'
test_suite.rationale: If can't fit toy data, gradient descent fundamentally broken.

test_suite.description: Sigmoid should not overflow/underflow for extreme inputs
test_suite.code:
def test_sigmoid_stability():
    model = LogisticRegressionGD()
    
    # Extreme positive
    z_pos = np.array([100, 500, 1000])
    sig_pos = model._sigmoid(z_pos)
    assert np.all(sig_pos > 0.99), 'Sigmoid underflow for large positive z'
    assert np.all(np.isfinite(sig_pos)), 'Sigmoid overflow'
    
    # Extreme negative
    z_neg = np.array([-100, -500, -1000])
    sig_neg = model._sigmoid(z_neg)
    assert np.all(sig_neg < 0.01), 'Sigmoid underflow for large negative z'
    assert np.all(np.isfinite(sig_neg)), 'Sigmoid underflow'
test_suite.rationale: Numerical stability critical. Without clipping, exp(1000) = ∞, exp(-1000) = 0 (underflow).

extended_nodes_v2.label: Debugging Non-Convergence Issues
extended_nodes_v2.description: Step-by-step debugging guide when gradient descent fails to converge
symptoms: Loss plateaus at high value (e.g., 0.69 for binary classification)

root_causes: Learning rate too low (e.g., 1e-6) → Updates too small
Features not scaled → Gradients dominated by large-scale features
Weights initialized to zeros → Symmetry prevents learning
solution: Check weight initialization: theta should be small random values, not zeros
Print gradient norm: If ||∇L|| < 1e-6, gradients vanishing
debugging_checklist.diagnostic_code: print(f'Gradient norm: {np.linalg.norm(gradient):.6f}'); print(f'Weight std: {np.std(model.theta):.6f}'); print(f'Feature mean: {X.mean(axis=0)}'); print(f'Feature std: {X.std(axis=0)}')

debugging_checklist.diagnosis: Learning rate too high. Overshooting optimal weights.
solution: Implement learning rate decay: α_t = α_0 / (1 + decay_rate * t)
Use adaptive optimizers: Adam, RMSprop (adjust lr per parameter)
debugging_checklist.diagnostic_code: if epoch > 10 and abs(loss_history[-1] - loss_history[-10]) < 0.01: print('Warning: Loss oscillating. Reduce learning rate.')

root_causes: Learning rate too high → weights explode
solution: Add clipping: z = np.clip(z, -500, 500) in sigmoid
Add epsilon in loss: log(pred + 1e-15) instead of log(pred)
Check weight magnitudes: If ||theta|| > 100, weights exploding
debugging_checklist.diagnostic_code: print(f'Max |z|: {np.abs(z).max():.2f}'); print(f'Weight norm: {np.linalg.norm(model.theta):.2f}'); print(f'Min pred: {predictions.min():.2e}, Max pred: {predictions.max():.2e}')

debugging_checklist.diagnosis: Features not normalized or learning rate suboptimal.
solution: Apply StandardScaler: (x - μ) / σ before training
Tune learning rate: Try [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0] via grid search
Check feature scales: If one feature ranges [0, 1000] and another [0, 1], gradient descent struggles

extended_nodes_v2.api_docs:
# Threshold Tuning Module

## Overview
Optimizes classification threshold to meet business constraints (e.g., FPR ≤ 5%).

## Installation
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt  # Includes numpy, scikit-learn
```

## Quick Start
```python
from src.evaluation import ThresholdOptimizer
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

# Assume trained model
y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]  # Probabilities for positive class

# Optimize threshold
optimizer = ThresholdOptimizer(
    constraint='fpr',  # Constraint type: 'fpr', 'precision', 'f1'
    constraint_value=0.05,  # FPR ≤ 5%
    n_thresholds=1000  # Granularity
)

optimal_threshold, metrics = optimizer.fit(y_val, y_proba)

print(f'Optimal threshold: {optimal_threshold:.3f}')
print(f'Recall at threshold: {metrics["recall"]:.3f}')
print(f'FPR at threshold: {metrics["fpr"]:.3f}')
```

## API Reference

### `ThresholdOptimizer`
Optimizes classification threshold subject to constraints.

#### Parameters
- **constraint** : str, {'fpr', 'precision', 'f1', 'specificity'}
  - Type of constraint to enforce.
  - 'fpr': False positive rate (FP / (FP + TN))
  - 'precision': Positive predictive value (TP / (TP + FP))
  - 'f1': Harmonic mean of precision and recall
  - 'specificity': True negative rate (TN / (TN + FP))

- **constraint_value** : float, range [0, 1]
  - Maximum allowed value for constraint metric.
  - Example: constraint='fpr', constraint_value=0.05 → FPR ≤ 5%

- **n_thresholds** : int, default=1000
  - Number of threshold candidates to evaluate.
  - Range: [0.0, 1.0] divided into `n_thresholds` equal steps.
  - Higher values → finer granularity but slower computation.

- **optimize_for** : str, {'recall', 'precision', 'f1'}, default='recall'
  - Metric to maximize subject to constraint.
  - Example: Maximize recall while keeping FPR ≤ 5%.

#### Methods

##### `fit(y_true, y_proba)`
Finds optimal threshold.

**Parameters:**
- **y_true** : array-like, shape (n_samples,)
  - Ground truth binary labels (0 or 1).
- **y_proba** : array-like, shape (n_samples,)
  - Predicted probabilities for positive class.

**Returns:**
- **threshold** : float
  - Optimal classification threshold.
- **metrics** : dict
  - Performance metrics at optimal threshold.
  - Keys: 'recall', 'precision', 'fpr', 'f1', 'specificity'

**Raises:**
- **ValueError** : If no threshold satisfies constraint.
  - Example: If FPR ≤ 5% impossible with current model, raises error.

**Example:**
```python
optimizer = ThresholdOptimizer(constraint='fpr', constraint_value=0.05)
threshold, metrics = optimizer.fit(y_val, y_proba)

if metrics['recall'] < 0.70:
    print('Warning: Recall below 70% target. Consider feature engineering.')
```

##### `plot_tradeoff_curve(y_true, y_proba, save_path=None)`
Visualizes recall-FPR trade-off across thresholds.

**Parameters:**
- **y_true** : array-like, shape (n_samples,)
- **y_proba** : array-like, shape (n_samples,)
- **save_path** : str, optional
  - Path to save plot. If None, displays interactively.

**Returns:**
- **fig** : matplotlib.figure.Figure
  - Figure object for further customization.

**Example:**
```python
optimizer.plot_tradeoff_curve(
    y_val, y_proba,
    save_path='results/threshold_tradeoff.png'
)
```

## Advanced Usage

### Multiple Constraints
Enforce both FPR ≤ 5% AND precision ≥ 80%:

```python
from src.evaluation import MultiConstraintOptimizer

optimizer = MultiConstraintOptimizer(
    constraints=[
        ('fpr', 0.05),      # FPR ≤ 5%
        ('precision', 0.80)  # Precision ≥ 80%
    ],
    optimize_for='recall'
)

try:
    threshold, metrics = optimizer.fit(y_val, y_proba)
    print(f'Threshold: {threshold:.3f}, Recall: {metrics["recall"]:.3f}')
except ValueError as e:
    print(f'Constraints infeasible: {e}')
    print('Consider: (1) Feature engineering, (2) Relaxing constraints, (3) Ensemble methods')
```

### Cost-Sensitive Threshold Selection
Select threshold minimizing business cost:

```python
# Define costs
cost_fp = 500   # $500 per false positive (user churn)
cost_fn = 2000  # $2000 per false negative (fraud loss)

optimizer = ThresholdOptimizer(constraint=None)  # No hard constraint
threshold, metrics = optimizer.fit_cost_sensitive(
    y_val, y_proba,
    cost_fp=cost_fp,
    cost_fn=cost_fn
)

print(f'Cost-optimal threshold: {threshold:.3f}')
print(f'Expected cost per 1000 users: ${metrics["expected_cost"]:.0f}')
```

## Performance Considerations

- **Computation time**: O(n_thresholds × n_samples)
  - For n_thresholds=1000, n_samples=10,000: ~0.5 seconds
- **Memory usage**: O(n_thresholds)
  - Stores threshold sweep results (negligible)

## Troubleshooting

### Error: "No threshold satisfies constraint"
**Cause**: Model cannot achieve constraint (e.g., FPR ≤ 5%) at any threshold.

**Solutions**:
1. Relax constraint (e.g., FPR ≤ 10%)
2. Improve model (feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning)
3. Check validation set: Is it representative of production data?

### Warning: "Optimal threshold at boundary (0.0 or 1.0)"
**Cause**: Constraint so loose that boundary threshold is optimal.

**Example**: FPR ≤ 50% constraint → threshold=0.0 (predict all positive) satisfies it.

**Solution**: Tighten constraint to meaningful business requirement.

## References

- [Threshold Selection for Binary Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08644)
- [Cost-Sensitive Learning](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1007663713082)
- [SHAP Documentation](https://shap.readthedocs.io/) for explainability

extended_nodes_v2.label: SMOTE Oversampling (Rejected)
extended_nodes_v2.description: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) was considered but rejected. Here's why.
extended_nodes_v2.approach: SMOTE generates synthetic minority class samples via k-nearest neighbors interpolation to balance 55:45 class distribution to 50:50.
extended_nodes_v2.implementation_tested: from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE; smote = SMOTE(sampling_strategy=1.0, k_neighbors=5, random_state=42); X_resampled, y_resampled = smote.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)

why_rejected.reason: Marginal recall improvement (+1-2 pp) not worth FPR increase (+2 pp)
why_rejected.quantification: SMOTE improves recall 81.2% → 82.9% but worsens FPR 21.9% → 23.8%. Net business impact negative: Catch 17 more attacks (good) but trigger 190 more false alarms (bad). At $500 churn per FP, cost increase = $95K > $34K fraud prevention. ROI negative.

why_rejected.reason: Synthetic samples not representative of real attacks
why_rejected.explanation: SMOTE interpolates between existing phishing samples. Example: If two phishing sites have DomainAge=3mo and 5mo, SMOTE creates synthetic sample with DomainAge=4mo. But real phishing attacks have discrete patterns (fresh domains <1mo, or aged domains >2yr bought from marketplaces). Interpolated 4mo samples mislead model.

why_rejected.observation: Train AUC: 0.92 (with SMOTE) vs 0.89 (baseline). Val AUC: 0.881 (with SMOTE) vs 0.888 (baseline). Gap widens: 0.92 - 0.881 = 0.039 (SMOTE) vs 0.89 - 0.888 = 0.002 (baseline). SMOTE causes overfitting to synthetic patterns that don't generalize.

why_rejected.guideline: SMOTE most beneficial for severe imbalance (>90:10). At 55:45, stratified sampling sufficient. Literature (Chawla et al., 2002) recommends SMOTE only when minority class <30%.

extended_nodes_v2.alternative_considered: ADASYN (Adaptive Synthetic Sampling): Generates more synthetic samples in regions where minority class is sparse. Tested: Results similar to SMOTE (marginal recall gain, FPR increase). Also rejected.
extended_nodes_v2.correct_approach: Stratified splits preserve natural distribution + threshold tuning optimizes operating point. More principled than artificially balancing via synthetic data.
extended_nodes_v2.lesson_learned: Don't default to SMOTE just because 'imbalance exists.' Quantify business impact: Does recall improvement justify FPR increase? In this case, no.
